name: What happens if hidden damage is found during demolition?

mainEntity.name: How should a commercial general contractor handle rot, mold, asbestos, or bad framing discovered during demolition?
mainEntity.text: How should a commercial general contractor handle rot, mold, asbestos, or bad framing discovered during demolition?

acceptedAnswer.text: Hidden conditions are common in older commercial spaces, especially when demolition exposes outdated framing, moisture damage, electrical issues, or unsafe materials. The correct response is to document the condition, notify the owner, protect the area, and determine whether testing or specialty removal is needed. In many cases, only the affected portion should stop so the rest of the job can continue. A good contractor does not turn every surprise into a full shutdown; instead, they separate urgent safety issues from ordinary scope growth. Owners should ask how the contractor handles concealed conditions, whether they bring in the right specialists, and how quickly they can produce a revised cost and schedule impact. If the contractor lacks a clear process, a hidden-condition discovery can quickly become a major delay and budget overrun.
acceptedAnswer.description: Hidden conditions should be documented immediately, isolated if needed, and priced through a written change process before replacement work continues. Demolition surprises are common in older commercial buildings and can affect schedule, safety, and budget. The contractor should stop only the affected area, not the entire project, whenever possible.
